# Results -- Study 514 (Pastor-Stambaugh Liquidity Risk) on real yfinance panel

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Protocol: build an
Amihud-style aggregate market-liquidity series, estimate each name's trailing 36-month
liquidity beta (loading on the liquidity shock, controlling for the market), sort the
cross-section monthly, and hold a dollar-neutral long high-gamma / short low-gamma book
with one execution lag. As-of **2026-06-26**.*

## Data stamp

| Frame | Shape | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|
| Close (daily adjusted) | 4023 days x 45 tickers | `1060fab16f5d` |
| Dollar-volume (Close x Volume) | 4023 days x 45 tickers | `7157e92920a6` |
| SPY (market proxy) | 4023 days | `5af4907fc2a8` |
| Period covered | 2010-01-04 -- 2025-12-30 | -- |

**Source:** yfinance daily adjusted-close prices (auto_adjust=True) and raw volume.
Universe: 45 large-cap names (current membership projected backwards). The panel is
survivorship-biased.

**Survivorship bias (named explicitly):** only companies that survived to 2026 are in
the sample. The natural *source* of liquidity risk -- small, thinly-traded, and
ultimately delisted names -- is absent. The aggregate-liquidity series is measured on
45 of the most liquid stocks on earth, which understates true liquidity-shock
dispersion. All positive results are **upper-bound estimates**.

## The honest test -- liquidity-risk sort

Aggregate liquidity = sign-flipped, z-scored cross-sectional average of monthly Amihud
illiquidity (mean daily |return| / dollar-volume). The liquidity *shock* is its monthly
first difference. Each name's liquidity beta gamma is the loading on the shock in a
trailing 36-month regression that also controls for the market excess return. Each month
we rank by trailing gamma (signal public at the prior month-end close, **one execution
lag**), go long the top-gamma tertile and short the bottom-gamma tertile, equal-weight,
dollar-neutral, and hold one month. Risk-free rate = 3%/yr constant (no FRED).

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| N months | 155 (2013-02 -- 2025-12) |
| Mean return (annualised, **gross**) | **+4.28%/yr** |
| Vol (annualised) | 11.81%/yr |
| Sharpe (annual, gross) | +0.362 |
| **HAC t-stat (gross)** | **+1.466** |
| Hit rate (months > 0) | 55.5% |
| Max drawdown | -19.8% |
| Long leg (high-gamma, ann) | +23.71%/yr |
| Short leg (low-gamma, ann) | +19.43%/yr |
| Avg one-way turnover (both legs) | 0.21 |

- High-gamma stocks earn **+4.28%/yr** more than low-gamma stocks, in the **direction**
  Pastor-Stambaugh (2003) predict -- but the HAC *t* = **+1.466** is below the inference
  bar of |*t*| >= 2. The premium is **not** statistically distinguishable from zero on
  this 13-year large-cap survivor panel.
- Both legs earn strongly positive raw returns (large-caps in a bull market); the
  long-short premium is the thin difference between them.

## Costs

One-way 10 bps x NAV x turnover on both legs each rebalance, plus 50 bps/yr borrow on
the short leg (pro-rated monthly).

| Statistic | Gross | Net |
|---|---|---|
| Mean return (ann) | +4.28%/yr | **+3.52%/yr** |
| Sharpe (ann) | +0.362 | +0.298 |
| HAC t-stat | +1.466 | **+1.207** |

Costs shave ~0.76%/yr. Turnover is low (0.21 one-way, because gamma is a slow-moving
36-month loading), so costs are not the killer here -- the gross signal already fails
the bar.

## Robustness

**Placebo (label-shuffle null, 200 permutations):** shuffle the gamma labels across
names each month and re-sort.

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Real long-short mean (ann) | +4.28%/yr |
| Placebo mean (ann) | -0.20%/yr |
| Placebo std (ann) | 2.37%/yr |
| **Two-sided p-value** | **0.070** |

The placebo null is centred on zero (the engine is unbiased), and the real signal sits
~1.8 placebo-sigma out -- *p* = 0.070, suggestive but above the 0.05 line and consistent
with the sub-2 HAC *t*.

**Liquidity-beta window sweep:**

| Window | Mean (ann) | HAC t | N |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 24 months | +3.46%/yr | +1.019 | 167 |
| 36 months | +4.28%/yr | +1.466 | 155 |
| 48 months | +2.81%/yr | +0.820 | 143 |

**Sort breadth:**

| Breadth | Mean (ann) | HAC t | N |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Tertile (top/bottom 1/3) | +4.28%/yr | +1.466 | 155 |
| Quintile (top/bottom 1/5) | +3.34%/yr | +0.799 | 155 |

Every variant is positive and in the predicted direction, but **none clears |t| >= 2.**
The signal is fragile to reasonable design choices.

## Synthetic positive control (engine faithfulness -- NOT a real-tape claim)

Plant a known liquidity-risk premium and verify the engine recovers it monotonically.

| Planted premium | LS mean (ann) | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|
| -0.08 | -11.98%/yr | -2.722 |
| 0.00 | -0.38%/yr | -0.087 |
| +0.06 | +8.22%/yr | +1.864 |
| +0.12 | +17.22%/yr | +3.824 |

The engine is faithful: zero at the null, monotone in the planted premium, correct sign,
clear *t* > 2 at a strong premium. So the marginal real-tape verdict reflects **the
market**, not a broken detector. (This control is a power check only -- it never
licenses a real-tape stamp.)

## Verdict

- **Signal -- WEAK.** Gross HAC *t* = +1.466 (|t| < 2) on 155 months of large-cap
  survivors; placebo *p* = 0.070. The premium is in the Pastor-Stambaugh (2003) direction
  (high-gamma out-earns low-gamma by +4.3%/yr) and the label-shuffle null is centred on
  zero, but the effect does not independently clear the bar. WEAK rather than NONE because
  the direction is right, the placebo is suggestive, and the original paper provides a
  strong prior on a broad CRSP universe.
- **Tradability -- FRAGILE.** Net +3.52%/yr, Sharpe +0.298, max drawdown -19.8%. Costs
  are mild (slow-moving gamma -> low turnover), but the net *t* = +1.207 is well below 2,
  and the signal is fragile to window and breadth choices.
- **Survivorship / does it survive the honest gauntlet? -- BUSTED.** The universe is
  45 of the most liquid stocks alive, projected backwards: the natural carriers of
  liquidity risk (illiquid, delisted, distressed names) are absent, so this is the most
  favourable possible test -- and it still fails |t| >= 2 net of costs. On a complete
  universe with real delistings the premium would more likely shrink than grow.
